book_title: The Lost Love of Akbar Manzil
subject_line: The old seaside house in The Lost Love of Akbar Manzil
email_body:
Dear Shubnum,

I was struck by how The Lost Love of Akbar Manzil grows out of Durban itself: you've described the city's coast as full of strange, grand houses that have aged into dilapidation, rather than one house you modelled the mansion on.

I'd love to ask how, over roughly eight years of writing, the love story you set out to tell became a whole life story.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. The portrait is developed through a few written questions, which you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

Would you be open to taking part? No pressure either way.

Best regards,
The Author Ledger
hook_note: LAPL interview: Akbar Manzil not modelled on a single Durban house; ~8 years to write; Durban Local on love story vs life story; won 2025 Sunday Times fiction award and joint UJ Main Prize.

subject_line: The years 2016 to 2018 in The Comrade's Wife
email_body:
Dear Barbara,

The Comrade's Wife caught my attention for its timing: a novel set between 2016 and 2018 that follows rising class status and the promises of transformation and democracy - what you called, at its UCT Writers Series launch, a romance with plots and subplots.

I'd be curious how you balance the romance with the political story, and how your work on Black South African women's novels feeds into your fiction.

book_title: Morafe: Person, Family and Nation in Colonial Bechuanaland, 1880s-1950s
email_body:
Dear Khumisho,

subject_line: A poetry debut and the UJ Prize: Weeping Becomes a River
email_body:
Dear Siphokazi,

Weeping Becomes a River winning the 2025 UJ Debut Prize stayed with me, partly because poetry collections so seldom take that award. A debut in verse being read alongside novels and memoirs says something about the book.

I'd like to ask about the title image of weeping that becomes a river, and how you shaped the collection's movement from one poem to the next.

book_title: One Hundred Years of Dispossession: My Family's Quest to Reclaim Our Land
subject_line: Your family's land claim in One Hundred Years of Dispossession
email_body:
Dear Lebogang,

One Hundred Years of Dispossession caught my attention because it tells the long story of land loss through your own family's effort to reclaim its land. I saw it was shortlisted for the 2025 Sunday Times non-fiction award.

I'd like to ask how you decided what to include from your family's memories, and how writing it changed your sense of the claim itself.
